claim: The hippocampus is critical for episodic and spatial memory formation.
source: The hippocampus is critical for episodic and spatial memory formation (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Squire, 1992; Tonegawa et al., 2015), but the neural computations underlying these functions are not well understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Squire, 1992; Tonegawa et al., 2015

claim: The trisynaptic circuit linking entorhinal cortex (EC) to dentate gyrus (DG), DG to CA3, and CA3 to CA1 is believed to endow the hippocampus with its functional capabilities.
source: The trisynaptic circuit linking entorhinal cortex (EC) to dentate gyrus (DG), DG to CA3, and CA3 to CA1 is believed to endow the hippocampus with its functional capabilities.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding of hippocampal circuitry

claim: The trisynaptic circuit was first described in the anatomical studies of Ramon y Cajal over a century ago.
source: Since the circuit was first described in the anatomical studies of Ramon y Cajal over a century ago (Ramon, 1911), considerable work has focused on each of the major hippocampal subfields (CA1-3 and DG) to identify their roles in hippocampal processing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramon, 1911

claim: Hippocampal subfields have related, but distinct roles in pattern separation and completion.
source: The resulting body of literature has indicated that the subfields have related, but distinct roles in pattern separation and completion (Gilbert et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Leutgeb et al., 2007; McHugh et al., 2007; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Kheirbek et al., 2013; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014; Rennó-Costa et al., 2014), response to novelty (Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008; Kemere et al., 2013; Larkin et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2021), and the encoding of social variables (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Okuyama et al., 2016; Meira et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Hippocampal subfields have roles in response to novelty.
source: The resulting body of literature has indicated that the subfields have related, but distinct roles in pattern separation and completion (Gilbert et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Leutgeb et al., 2007; McHugh et al., 2007; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Kheirbek et al., 2013; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014; Rennó-Costa et al., 2014), response to novelty (Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008; Kemere et al., 2013; Larkin et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2021), and the encoding of social variables (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Okuyama et al., 2016; Meira et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008; Kemere et al., 2013; Larkin et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2021

claim: Hippocampal subfields have roles in the encoding of social variables.
source: The resulting body of literature has indicated that the subfields have related, but distinct roles in pattern separation and completion (Gilbert et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Leutgeb et al., 2007; McHugh et al., 2007; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Kheirbek et al., 2013; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014; Rennó-Costa et al., 2014), response to novelty (Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008; Kemere et al., 2013; Larkin et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2021), and the encoding of social variables (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Okuyama et al., 2016; Meira et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Okuyama et al., 2016; Meira et al., 2018

claim: There are differences between hippocampal subfields in the stability of their place fields.
source: Additionally, there appear to be differences between the subfields in the stability of their place fields (Dong et al., 2021; Mankin et al., 2012; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2021; Mankin et al., 2012; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018

claim: Electrophysiology has been the principal tool used to study the hippocampus.
source: Historically, electrophysiology has been the principal tool used to study the hippocampus.
evidence: Based on historical scientific practice

claim: Electrophysiological recordings have the advantage of high temporal resolution and can directly measure spiking.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have the advantage of high temporal resolution and can directly measure spiking, but they are typically limited to small numbers of neurons in particular subfields.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of electrophysiology capabilities

claim: Electrophysiological recordings are typically limited to small numbers of neurons in particular subfields.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have the advantage of high temporal resolution and can directly measure spiking, but they are typically limited to small numbers of neurons in particular subfields.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of electrophysiology limitations

claim: Localization of recorded neurons within the hippocampus using electrophysiology is approximate, requiring post hoc histological analysis.
source: Additionally, localization of recorded neurons within the hippocampus is approximate, requiring post hoc histological analysis to estimate the position of the electrode tracks, with the distances between the recorded neurons and the electrode sites being poorly defined.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of electrophysiology limitations

claim: Calcium imaging approaches have been used to record hippocampal activity in recent years.
source: In recent years, calcium imaging approaches (i.e. single-photon mini-endoscopes and two-photon [2P] microscopy) have been used to record hippocampal activity, allowing for the simultaneous measurement of large numbers of neurons with known spatial relationships (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Dombeck et al., 2010; Ghosh et al., 2011; Ziv et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2016; Sheintuch et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Dombeck et al., 2010; Ghosh et al., 2011; Ziv et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2016; Sheintuch et al., 2017

claim: Calcium imaging approaches allow for the simultaneous measurement of large numbers of neurons with known spatial relationships.
source: In recent years, calcium imaging approaches (i.e. single-photon mini-endoscopes and two-photon [2P] microscopy) have been used to record hippocampal activity, allowing for the simultaneous measurement of large numbers of neurons with known spatial relationships (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Dombeck et al., 2010; Ghosh et al., 2011; Ziv et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2016; Sheintuch et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Calcium imaging approaches for hippocampal recording require aspiration of the overlying neocortex.
source: However, these approaches require aspiration of the overlying neocortex and are generally restricted to a single subfield for each animal.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of calcium imaging procedures

claim: Calcium imaging approaches for hippocampal recording are generally restricted to a single subfield for each animal.
source: However, these approaches require aspiration of the overlying neocortex and are generally restricted to a single subfield for each animal.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of calcium imaging limitations

claim: A procedure for transverse imaging of the trisynaptic hippocampal circuit using chronically implanted glass microperiscopes was developed.
source: To address these challenges, we have developed a procedure for transverse imaging of the trisynaptic hippocampal circuit using chronically implanted glass microperiscopes.
evidence: This is the main methodological contribution of the study

claim: Neural tissue remained intact and healthy for prolonged periods of time (up to 10 months) with implanted microprisms.
source: As has been found with previous studies using implanted microprisms in cortex (Chia and Levene, 2009; Andermann et al., 2013; Low et al., 2014), the neural tissue remained intact and healthy for prolonged periods of time (up to 10 months), and both dendritic structure and calcium activity could be repeatedly measured in awake mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chia and Levene, 2009; Andermann et al., 2013; Low et al., 2014, and by data from the current study

claim: Both dendritic structure and calcium activity could be repeatedly measured in awake mice using the microperiscope approach.
source: As has been found with previous studies using implanted microprisms in cortex (Chia and Levene, 2009; Andermann et al., 2013; Low et al., 2014), the neural tissue remained intact and healthy for prolonged periods of time (up to 10 months), and both dendritic structure and calcium activity could be repeatedly measured in awake mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study

claim: Axial resolution is decreased compared to traditional cranial windows when using the microperiscope.
source: Optical modeling and point spread function (PSF) measurements showed that axial resolution is decreased compared to traditional cranial windows, but is sufficient to image individual apical dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons several millimeters below the pial surface.
evidence: Demonstrated by optical modeling and PSF measurements in the study

claim: The microperiscope approach is sufficient to image individual apical dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons several millimeters below the pial surface.
source: Optical modeling and point spread function (PSF) measurements showed that axial resolution is decreased compared to traditional cranial windows, but is sufficient to image individual apical dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons several millimeters below the pial surface.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study

claim: Spine turnover in CA1 apical dendrites was quantified across days using the microperiscope approach.
source: Using this approach, we quantified spine turnover in CA1 apical dendrites across days.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study

claim: Neurons in CA1, CA3, and DG were found whose activity met criteria to be considered place cells.
source: We found neurons in all regions whose activity met criteria to be considered place cells (PCs) and speed cells (SCs).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study

claim: Neurons in CA1, CA3, and DG were found whose activity met criteria to be considered speed cells.
source: We found neurons in all regions whose activity met criteria to be considered place cells (PCs) and speed cells (SCs).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study

claim: A non-uniform distribution of spatial information was found across the extent of the DG-to-CA1 axis.
source: Further, we found a non-uniform distribution of spatial information across the extent of the DG-to-CA1 axis, supporting findings from earlier electrophysiological studies that found similar heterogeneity (Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study and supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015

claim: Earlier electrophysiological studies found heterogeneity in spatial information across the DG-to-CA1 axis.
source: Further, we found a non-uniform distribution of spatial information across the extent of the DG-to-CA1 axis, supporting findings from earlier electrophysiological studies that found similar heterogeneity (Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015

claim: Two types of microperiscopes were used: v1CA1 (1 × 1 × 2 mm³) for imaging CA1 only, and v2HPC (1.5 × 1.5 × 2.5 mm³) for imaging the entire transverse hippocampus.
source: For imaging CA1 only, we used a 1 × 1 × 2 mm3 microperiscope (v1CA1; Figure 1B, left), and for imaging the entire transverse hippocampus (CA1-CA3, DG), we used a 1.5 × 1.5 × 2.5 mm3 microperiscope (v2HPC; Figure 1B, right).
evidence: Describes the experimental methods used in the study

claim: The microperiscope hypotenuse was coated with enhanced aluminum to reflect the imaging plane orthogonally onto the transverse plane.
source: The microperiscope hypotenuse was coated with enhanced aluminum in order to reflect the imaging plane orthogonally onto the transverse plane (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Describes the experimental methods used in the study

claim: Microperiscope implantation eliminated the need for aspiration of cortical tissue typically performed prior to hippocampal imaging.
source: Although this approach eliminated the need for the aspiration of cortical tissue typically performed prior to hippocampal imaging (Dombeck et al., 2010), it nonetheless results in severed connections and compressed tissue medial to the implant.
evidence: Describes the experimental approach and cites Dombeck et al., 2010 for comparison

claim: Microperiscope implantation results in severed connections and compressed tissue medial to the implant.
source: Although this approach eliminated the need for the aspiration of cortical tissue typically performed prior to hippocampal imaging (Dombeck et al., 2010), it nonetheless results in severed connections and compressed tissue medial to the implant.
evidence: Describes the consequences of the experimental approach

claim: An increase in the prevalence of astrocytes was found close to the microperiscope face.
source: Similar to previous research using microprism implants (Andermann et al., 2013), we found an increase in the prevalence of astrocytes close to the microperiscope face, but the density decreased with distance and was indistinguishable from the control hemisphere beyond 300 μm from the microperiscope face (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F and supported by citation to Andermann et al., 2013

claim: Astrocyte density decreased with distance from the microperiscope face and was indistinguishable from the control hemisphere beyond 300 μm.
source: Similar to previous research using microprism implants (Andermann et al., 2013), we found an increase in the prevalence of astrocytes close to the microperiscope face, but the density decreased with distance and was indistinguishable from the control hemisphere beyond 300 μm from the microperiscope face (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Signal intensity imaged through the v1CA1 microperiscope was reduced to 59.0% ± 6.6% compared to a standard coverslip.
source: We found that signal intensity imaged through the microperiscope was reduced compared to a standard coverslip (v1CA1 microperiscope: 59.0% ± 6.6%; v2HPC microperiscope: 67.2% ± 8.5%; mean ±s.d.; Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: Signal intensity imaged through the v2HPC microperiscope was reduced to 67.2% ± 8.5% compared to a standard coverslip.
source: We found that signal intensity imaged through the microperiscope was reduced compared to a standard coverslip (v1CA1 microperiscope: 59.0% ± 6.6%; v2HPC microperiscope: 67.2% ± 8.5%; mean ±s.d.; Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: The lateral FWHM for a standard coverslip was 0.6 μm.
source: Compared to a standard cranial window using a 0.15 mm coverslip, we found that the FWHM was higher for both lateral (coverslip: 0.6 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 1.0 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 0.8 μm; Figure 2D–G) and axial (coverslip: 3.4 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 11.7 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 9.5 μm; Figure 2D–G) dimensions.
evidence: Demonstrated by PSF measurements shown in Figure 2D-G

claim: The lateral FWHM for the v1CA1 microperiscope was 1.0 μm.
source: Compared to a standard cranial window using a 0.15 mm coverslip, we found that the FWHM was higher for both lateral (coverslip: 0.6 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 1.0 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 0.8 μm; Figure 2D–G) and axial (coverslip: 3.4 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 11.7 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 9.5 μm; Figure 2D–G) dimensions.
evidence: Demonstrated by PSF measurements shown in Figure 2D-G

claim: The lateral FWHM for the v2HPC microperiscope was 0.8 μm.
source: Compared to a standard cranial window using a 0.15 mm coverslip, we found that the FWHM was higher for both lateral (coverslip: 0.6 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 1.0 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 0.8 μm; Figure 2D–G) and axial (coverslip: 3.4 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 11.7 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 9.5 μm; Figure 2D–G) dimensions.
evidence: Demonstrated by PSF measurements shown in Figure 2D-G

claim: The axial FWHM for a standard coverslip was 3.4 μm.
source: Compared to a standard cranial window using a 0.15 mm coverslip, we found that the FWHM was higher for both lateral (coverslip: 0.6 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 1.0 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 0.8 μm; Figure 2D–G) and axial (coverslip: 3.4 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 11.7 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 9.5 μm; Figure 2D–G) dimensions.
evidence: Demonstrated by PSF measurements shown in Figure 2D-G

claim: The axial FWHM for the v1CA1 microperiscope was 11.7 μm.
source: Compared to a standard cranial window using a 0.15 mm coverslip, we found that the FWHM was higher for both lateral (coverslip: 0.6 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 1.0 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 0.8 μm; Figure 2D–G) and axial (coverslip: 3.4 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 11.7 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 9.5 μm; Figure 2D–G) dimensions.
evidence: Demonstrated by PSF measurements shown in Figure 2D-G

claim: The axial FWHM for the v2HPC microperiscope was 9.5 μm.
source: Compared to a standard cranial window using a 0.15 mm coverslip, we found that the FWHM was higher for both lateral (coverslip: 0.6 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 1.0 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 0.8 μm; Figure 2D–G) and axial (coverslip: 3.4 μm; v1CA1 microperiscope: 11.7 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 9.5 μm; Figure 2D–G) dimensions.
evidence: Demonstrated by PSF measurements shown in Figure 2D-G

claim: The decrease in resolution is predominantly due to clipping of the excitation beam, resulting in a reduction of the functional numerical aperture of the imaging system.
source: Optical modeling indicated that the decrease in resolution is predominantly due to clipping of the excitation beam, resulting in a reduction of the functional numerical aperture of the imaging system (theoretical axial PSF FWHM of v1CA1 microperiscope: 10.9 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 7.7 μm; see Materials and methods) rather than optical aberrations.
evidence: Demonstrated by optical modeling in the study

claim: The theoretical axial PSF FWHM of the v1CA1 microperiscope is 10.9 μm.
source: Optical modeling indicated that the decrease in resolution is predominantly due to clipping of the excitation beam, resulting in a reduction of the functional numerical aperture of the imaging system (theoretical axial PSF FWHM of v1CA1 microperiscope: 10.9 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 7.7 μm; see Materials and methods) rather than optical aberrations.
evidence: Calculated from optical modeling

claim: The theoretical axial PSF FWHM of the v2HPC microperiscope is 7.7 μm.
source: Optical modeling indicated that the decrease in resolution is predominantly due to clipping of the excitation beam, resulting in a reduction of the functional numerical aperture of the imaging system (theoretical axial PSF FWHM of v1CA1 microperiscope: 10.9 μm; v2HPC microperiscope: 7.7 μm; see Materials and methods) rather than optical aberrations.
evidence: Calculated from optical modeling

claim: Use of adaptive optics did not significantly improve the axial resolution.
source: As a result, use of adaptive optics did not significantly improve the axial resolution, though adaptive optics did improve the signal intensity by 40–80% (data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental testing in the study

claim: Adaptive optics improved the signal intensity by 40–80%.
source: As a result, use of adaptive optics did not significantly improve the axial resolution, though adaptive optics did improve the signal intensity by 40–80% (data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental testing in the study

claim: The resolution was mostly uniform across the horizontal extent of the microperiscope.
source: We found that the resolution was mostly uniform, with no significant differences observed in lateral or axial resolution as a function of horizontal position (Figure 2I; lateral: F(14, 593)=0.53, p=0.91; axial: F(14, 593)=0.91, p=0.55; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis of PSF measurements shown in Figure 2I

claim: The lateral FWHM did not change as a function of distance from the microperiscope face.
source: The lateral FWHM did not change as a function of distance from the microperiscope face (Figure 2K; F(19, 109)=0.53, p=0.26; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis of PSF measurements shown in Figure 2K

claim: The axial FWHM slightly increased with greater distances from the microperiscope face.
source: The axial FWHM slightly increased with greater distances from the microperiscope face (Figure 2K; F(19, 109)=2.51, p=0.002; one-way ANOVA), though none of the individual positions were significantly different when corrected for multiple comparisons (p>0.05 for all positions, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis of PSF measurements shown in Figure 2K

claim: Imaging through the microperiscope lowers signal intensity and axial resolution.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that imaging through the microperiscope lowers signal intensity and axial resolution.
evidence: Inferred from the PSF and signal intensity measurements presented

claim: The quality of imaging through the microperiscope is sufficient to image individual HPC neurons and sub-micron morphological structures with laser power well below the photodamage threshold.
source: Despite these effects, the quality is still sufficient to image individual HPC neurons (Figure 1C) and sub-micron morphological structures (Figure 3) with laser power well below the photodamage threshold.
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figures 1C and 3

claim: Dendritic spines fall into four major morphological subtypes: filopodium, thin, mushroom, and stubby.
source: Previous studies have shown that dendritic spines fall into four major morphological subtypes: filopodium, thin, mushroom, and stubby (Chang and Greenough, 1984; Rodriguez et al., 2008; Son et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang and Greenough, 1984; Rodriguez et al., 2008; Son et al., 2011

claim: The distribution of dendritic spines was 30.4% thin, 41.0% stubby, 26.2% mushroom, and 2.3% filopodium.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found a non-uniform distribution of dendritic spines: 30.4% thin, 41.0% stubby, 26.2% mushroom, and 2.3% filopodium (F(3,100) = 51.47, p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA; Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3E

claim: The low proportion of filopodium found in 2P imaging and histological studies (2–3%) compared to electron microscopy studies (~7%) may result from the narrow width of these structures causing them to fall below the detection threshold.
source: The low proportion of filopodium found in this and previous 2P imaging and histological studies (Lendvai et al., 2000; Risher et al., 2014) (2–3%), as compared to electron microscopy studies (Fiala et al., 1998; Stewart et al., 2005) (~7%), may result from the narrow width of these structures causing them to fall below the detection threshold (Attardo et al., 2015; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2014; Castello-Waldow et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of different imaging modalities and supported by multiple citations

claim: Filopodium spines have a high turnover rate, while other classes are more stable across sessions.
source: Consistent with previous work (Grutzendler et al., 2002; Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Holtmaat et al., 2005), we found that particular classes, such as filopodium, had a high turnover rate, while other classes were more stable across sessions (F(3,100) = 7.17, p<0.001, one-way ANOVA; Figure 3F).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and supported by citations to Grutzendler et al., 2002; Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Holtmaat et al., 2005

claim: Total turnover dynamics reflect 15.0% ± 2.0% spine addition and 13.0% ± 1.9% spine subtraction across consecutive days.
source: We found that total turnover dynamics reflect 15.0% ± 2.0% spine addition and 13.0% ± 1.9% spine subtraction across consecutive days, representing a high degree of instability (Figure 3H, I).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3H and I

claim: Across 10 days, there was a 23.5% net loss in original spines.
source: Across 10 days, we found a 23.5% net loss in original spines, indicating that most spine turnover takes place within an isolated population of transient spines.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental measurements of survival fraction

claim: Most spine turnover takes place within an isolated population of transient spines.
source: Across 10 days, we found a 23.5% net loss in original spines, indicating that most spine turnover takes place within an isolated population of transient spines.
evidence: Inferred from the survival fraction and daily turnover data

claim: Cumulative turnover and survival fraction results were generally similar to previous findings from basal dendrites in CA1.
source: Both our cumulative turnover and survival fraction results were generally similar to previous findings from basal dendrites in CA1 (Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018), indicating that apical and basal dendrites exhibit similar spine dynamics.
evidence: Comparison with prior studies cited

claim: Apical and basal dendrites exhibit similar spine dynamics.
source: Both our cumulative turnover and survival fraction results were generally similar to previous findings from basal dendrites in CA1 (Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018), indicating that apical and basal dendrites exhibit similar spine dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of current results with prior studies

claim: The same dendritic processes could be identified over long time periods (up to 150 days).
source: Despite these limitations, we found that we could identify the same dendritic processes over long time periods (up to 150 days; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), allowing for longitudinal experiments tracking isolated dendritic structures over long time intervals.
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Neurons from CA1, CA3, and DG could be imaged in the same animal using the v2HPC microperiscope.
source: As with the Thy1-GFP-M mice, we were able to image neurons from CA1-CA3, and DG in the same animal (Figure 4A and B; Video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: In some cases, all three hippocampal areas (CA1, CA3, DG) could be recorded from simultaneously.
source: In some cases, depending on microperiscope placement, we were able to record from all three areas simultaneously (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Normal calcium dynamics with clear transients were found in all HPC subfields.
source: In all HPC subfields, we found normal calcium dynamics with clear transients (Figure 4C, D; Video 2 and Video 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: The imaging fields remained stable, and the same field could be imaged over 100 days later.
source: The imaging fields remained stable, and the same field could be imaged over 100 days later (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Microperiscope implantation allowed measurement of neural responses from mossy cells in the DG.
source: In addition, microperiscope implantation allowed measurement of neural responses from mossy cells in the DG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and, depending on microperiscope placement, simultaneous imaging of deep-layer cortical neurons in parietal cortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2

claim: Microperiscope implantation allowed simultaneous imaging of deep-layer cortical neurons in parietal cortex, depending on microperiscope placement.
source: In addition, microperiscope implantation allowed measurement of neural responses from mossy cells in the DG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and, depending on microperiscope placement, simultaneous imaging of deep-layer cortical neurons in parietal cortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: It remains unclear how similar rodent hippocampal activity in real-world environments is to that in VR.
source: Previous work has made use of virtual reality (VR) (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Dombeck et al., 2010), however it remains unclear how similar rodent hippocampal activity in real-world environments is to that in VR (Aronov and Tank, 2014; Aghajan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aronov and Tank, 2014; Aghajan et al., 2015

claim: The floating chamber approach lacks vestibular information present in real-world navigation but captures somatosensory and proprioceptive information missing from virtual environments.
source: Although this approach lacks the vestibular information present in real-world navigation, it captures somatosensory and proprioceptive information missing from virtual environments (Go et al., 2021; Aghajan et al., 2015; Ravassard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Go et al., 2021; Aghajan et al., 2015; Ravassard et al., 2013

claim: Place field width and single-cell spatial information using the floating chamber approach is comparable to the responses of free foraging animals.
source: Moreover, recent work has found that place field width and single-cell spatial information using this approach is comparable to the responses of free foraging animals (Go et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Go et al., 2021

claim: Using a curvilinear track allowed for robust sampling of the spatial environment and improved place field localization.
source: As found previously (Go et al., 2021), using a curvilinear track allowed for robust sampling of the spatial environment and improved place field localization, though they could also be measured in the open field.
evidence: Supported by citation to Go et al., 2021 and demonstrated by experimental approach

claim: 1001 neurons were recorded from CA1, 832 from CA3, and 463 from DG.
source: To characterize place fields, we recorded from neurons in CA1, CA3, and DG (CA1: n=1001; CA3: n=832; and DG: n=463) in transgenic mice with panexcitatory expression of GCaMP6s (Figure 5B; n=8 mice).
evidence: Describes the experimental data collected

claim: 26.0% of CA1 neurons, 18.9% of CA3 neurons, and 14.0% of DG neurons were identified as place cells.
source: The distribution was in general agreement with previous 2P imaging experiments in mice (Dong et al., 2021; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018) (Figure 5D and G; CA1: 26.0%; CA3: 18.9%; DG: 14.0%), with fields that spanned the entirety of the track (Figure 5F).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and G, and supported by citations to Dong et al., 2021; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018

claim: Place field widths were comparable across CA1, CA3, and DG.
source: We found that place field widths were comparable across the three regions (Figure 5H; CA1: mean (median) ± s.e.m.=18.8 (19.4) ±0.4 cm; CA3: 18.6 (18.8) ± 0.5 cm; DG: 18.9 (19.5) ±0.8 cm) and that spatial information was highest in CA1, followed by CA3, then DG (Figure 5I; CA1: mean (median) ± s.e.m.=0.95 (0.87) ± 0.03 bits/inferred spike; CA3: 0.89 (0.68) ± 0.05 bits/inferred spike; DG: 0.79 (0.61) ± 0.08 bits/inferred spike).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5H

claim: Spatial information was highest in CA1, followed by CA3, then DG.
source: We found that place field widths were comparable across the three regions (Figure 5H; CA1: mean (median) ± s.e.m.=18.8 (19.4) ±0.4 cm; CA3: 18.6 (18.8) ± 0.5 cm; DG: 18.9 (19.5) ±0.8 cm) and that spatial information was highest in CA1, followed by CA3, then DG (Figure 5I; CA1: mean (median) ± s.e.m.=0.95 (0.87) ± 0.03 bits/inferred spike; CA3: 0.89 (0.68) ± 0.05 bits/inferred spike; DG: 0.79 (0.61) ± 0.08 bits/inferred spike).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5I

claim: The place field width and spatial information of the CA1 PCs were similar to those found in a previous study using the same floating chamber design with a traditional hippocampal window implant.
source: The place field width and spatial information of the CA1 PCs were similar to those found in a previous study using the same floating chamber design with a traditional hippocampal window implant (Go et al., 2021).
evidence: Comparison with prior study cited

claim: PC width did not vary significantly as a function of depth of the imaging plane from the face of the microperiscope.
source: PC width did not vary significantly as a function of depth of the imaging plane from the face of the microperiscope (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; F(4, 241)=1.6, p=0.17, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Spatial information did vary as a function of depth from the microperiscope face, but there was no systematic effect.
source: Spatial information did vary as a function of depth (F(4, 1872)=15.9, p=8.6 × 10–13, one-way ANOVA), but there was no systematic effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Decay constant for the fitted transients had a significant relationship with imaging depth.
source: Decay constant for the fitted transients (Friedrich et al., 2017) did have a significant relationship with imaging depth (F(4, 1872)=29.8, p=4.5 × 10–24), which may be due to aberrant activity in a small subset of neurons close ( ≤ 130 μm) to the microperiscope face (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Cells responsive to speed have been found in the medial EC and CA1.
source: As cells responsive to speed have recently been found in the medial EC (Kropff et al., 2015; Iwase et al., 2020) and CA1 (Kropff et al., 2015; Iwase et al., 2020), we also identified neurons as SCs if their activity was significantly related to running speed (Kropff et al., 2015) (see Materials and methods; average speed per recording: CA1, 71.3 ± 33.7 mm/s; CA3, 76.2 ± 32.1; DG, 101.1 ± 49.0; Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test: CA1-CA3, p=0.90; CA3-DG, p=0.53; CA1-DG, p=0.32).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kropff et al., 2015; Iwase et al., 2020

claim: Speed cells were found in CA1, CA3, and DG, with all areas having cells that showed both increased and decreased activity with higher running speeds.
source: We found SCs in CA1, CA3, and DG, with all areas having cells that showed both increased and decreased activity with higher running speeds (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Speed cells were most abundant in DG (30.2%), compared to CA1 (9.4%) and CA3 (13.5%).
source: SCs were most abundant in DG (Figure 5G; CA1: 9.4%; CA3: 13.5%; DG: 30.2%), consistent with recent work that found it was possible to decode the speed of freely moving animals from the activity of DG, but not CA1 (Stefanini et al., 2020).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and supported by citation to Stefanini et al., 2020

claim: It is possible to decode the speed of freely moving animals from the activity of DG, but not CA1.
source: SCs were most abundant in DG (Figure 5G; CA1: 9.4%; CA3: 13.5%; DG: 30.2%), consistent with recent work that found it was possible to decode the speed of freely moving animals from the activity of DG, but not CA1 (Stefanini et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stefanini et al., 2020

claim: Place field width and spatial information have been found to vary among different subregions of CA3.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have indeed found that spatial information and place field width vary as a function of distance along the DG-to-CA1 axis (Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015), and that the most proximal part of CA3 is functionally more similar to DG than to the rest of CA3 (Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015

claim: Distal CA3 (dCA3) and CA2 have lower spatial information and larger place fields than medial CA3 (mCA3).
source: In particular, place field width and spatial information have been found to vary among different subregions of CA3, with distal CA3 (dCA3) and CA2 having lower spatial information and larger place fields than medial CA3 (mCA3) (Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015), and proximal CA3 (pCA3) having values most similar to DG (Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015

claim: Proximal CA3 (pCA3) has spatial information and place field width values most similar to DG.
source: In particular, place field width and spatial information have been found to vary among different subregions of CA3, with distal CA3 (dCA3) and CA2 having lower spatial information and larger place fields than medial CA3 (mCA3) (Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015), and proximal CA3 (pCA3) having values most similar to DG (Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014

claim: There are known anatomical gradients in connectivity of CA3.
source: Such distributions could be supported by known anatomical gradients in connectivity of CA3 (Claiborne et al., 1986; Ishizuka et al., 1990; Li et al., 1994; Ishizuka et al., 1995; Witter, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Claiborne et al., 1986; Ishizuka et al., 1990; Li et al., 1994; Ishizuka et al., 1995; Witter, 2007

claim: Several hundred cells (mean ± s.d.; 215 ± 74 neurons per recording; total: 1075 neurons) extending from pCA3 to pCA1 were simultaneously imaged using the v2HPC microperiscope.
source: Using the v2HPC microperiscope, we simultaneously imaged from several hundred cells (mean ± s.d.; 215 ± 74 neurons per recording; total: 1075 neurons) extending from pCA3 to pCA1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Describes the experimental data collected and shown in Figure 6A

claim: A non-uniform distribution of spatial information was found along the DG-to-CA1 axis.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015), we found a non-uniform distribution of spatial information along this axis (Figure 6B and C; F(4, 1047)=5.10, p=4.6 × 10–4; general linear F-test against a flat distribution with the same mean).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C, and supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015

claim: pCA3 cells had spatial information that was closer in value to those in DG than mCA3.
source: In particular, we found that pCA3 cells had spatial information that was closer in value to those in DG than mCA3 (Figure 6B and C; Figure 5I), and that mCA3 had spatial information that was greater than dCA3/CA2 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: mCA3 had spatial information that was greater than dCA3/CA2.
source: In particular, we found that pCA3 cells had spatial information that was closer in value to those in DG than mCA3 (Figure 6B and C; Figure 5I), and that mCA3 had spatial information that was greater than dCA3/CA2 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: Place field widths were narrowest in mCA3.
source: We found that place field widths were narrowest in mCA3, although we failed to find a statistically significant non-uniform distribution with respect to place field width across the extent of the DG-to-CA1 axis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; F(4, 206)=1.63, p=0.17, general linear F-test against a flat distribution with the same mean).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: No statistically significant non-uniform distribution was found with respect to place field width across the extent of the DG-to-CA1 axis.
source: We found that place field widths were narrowest in mCA3, although we failed to find a statistically significant non-uniform distribution with respect to place field width across the extent of the DG-to-CA1 axis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; F(4, 206)=1.63, p=0.17, general linear F-test against a flat distribution with the same mean).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The microperiscope allows for the recording from multiple hippocampal subfields simultaneously.
source: (1) The microperiscope allows for the recording from multiple hippocampal subfields simultaneously (Figure 6; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), allowing investigation of interactions between neurons in different subfields during behavior.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The microperiscope enables the investigation of local circuits by allowing morphological and genetic identification of different cell types.
source: (2) The microperiscope enables the investigation of local circuits by allowing morphological and genetic identification of different cell types.
evidence: Inferred from the capabilities demonstrated in the study

claim: The microperiscope can be combined with retrograde-transported viruses to allow projection-based cell identification.
source: (3) The microperiscope can be combined with retrograde-transported viruses to allow projection-based cell identification, making it possible to identify neurons that project to specific downstream targets.
evidence: Speculative application based on the method

claim: Neurons in ventral CA1 that project to the nucleus accumbens shell have been implicated in social memory.
source: Since hippocampal neurons that project to different brain regions have been found to exhibit distinct functional properties (e.g. neurons in ventral CA1 that project to the nucleus accumbens shell have been implicated in social memory; Okuyama et al., 2016), the union of these tools will be a powerful means for understanding hippocampal outputs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Okuyama et al., 2016

claim: The microperiscope provides access to the entire dendritic tree of pyramidal neurons.
source: (4) Finally, the microperiscope provides access to the entire dendritic tree of pyramidal neurons (Figures 1C, 3A and 5B; Video 2), giving optical access to dendritic signaling over a much larger spatial extent than has been previously possible (Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015; Sheffield et al., 2017; Adoff et al., 2021).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figures 1C, 3A, and 5B, and supported by citations to Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015; Sheffield et al., 2017; Adoff et al., 2021

claim: Dendritic spines are highly dynamic and motile structures that serve as the postsynaptic sites of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus.
source: Dendritic spines are highly dynamic and motile structures that serve as the postsynaptic sites of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Harris, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Harris, 1999

claim: Previous in vitro studies suggest a role for dendritic spines in structural and functional plasticity.
source: Previous in vitro studies suggest a role for dendritic spines in structural and functional plasticity, but the transient and dynamic nature of these structures make them ideally suited for being studied in vivo (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2001; Yang et al., 2009; Attardo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2001; Yang et al., 2009; Attardo et al., 2015

claim: Existing techniques allow imaging of spines on the basal CA1 dendrites near the surface of the hippocampus.
source: Although existing techniques allow imaging of spines on the basal CA1 dendrites near the surface of the hippocampus (Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018), as well as transverse offshoots of apical dendrites (Gu et al., 2014; Ulivi et al., 2019), imaging hippocampal neurons along the major somatodendritic axis has not previously been possible.
evidence: Supported by citations to Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2014; Ulivi et al., 2019

claim: Imaging hippocampal neurons along the major somatodendritic axis has not previously been possible.
source: Although existing techniques allow imaging of spines on the basal CA1 dendrites near the surface of the hippocampus (Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018), as well as transverse offshoots of apical dendrites (Gu et al., 2014; Ulivi et al., 2019), imaging hippocampal neurons along the major somatodendritic axis has not previously been possible.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: The Thy1-GFP-M mouse line has dense expression throughout DG.
source: Although it is theoretically possible to image DG dendritic structures using the microperiscope, the Thy1-GFP-M mouse line has dense expression throughout DG (Figure 1C and D), which prevented clear identification of distinct processes.
evidence: Observed in imaging data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Dense GFP expression in DG prevented clear identification of distinct dendritic processes.
source: Although it is theoretically possible to image DG dendritic structures using the microperiscope, the Thy1-GFP-M mouse line has dense expression throughout DG (Figure 1C and D), which prevented clear identification of distinct processes.
evidence: Inferred from the imaging observations

claim: Place cells are significantly less stable in the absence of reward.
source: Recent work has found that PCs are significantly less stable in the absence of reward (Krishnan et al., 2020; Pettit et al., 2022), which may explain the lower lap-wise reliability in our experiments compared to similar experiments using the same behavioral apparatus (Go et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krishnan et al., 2020; Pettit et al., 2022

claim: Reward is known to modulate hippocampal activity.
source: To assess the ability of our optical and behavioral experimental methods to capture spatial coding, we chose to measure place fields in the absence of reward, which is known to modulate hippocampal activity (Gauthier and Tank, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gauthier and Tank, 2018

claim: Electrophysiology has been the principal tool used to study the hippocampus over the past five decades.
source: Over the past five decades, electrophysiology has been the principal tool used to study the hippocampus.
evidence: Based on historical scientific practice

claim: Electrophysiology has much higher temporal resolution than calcium imaging.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have much higher temporal resolution than calcium imaging and can directly measure spikes, but have limited spatial resolution.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of electrophysiology and calcium imaging capabilities

claim: The microperiscope approach allows large scale imaging of neurons across multiple hippocampal subfields, with known spatial and morphological relationships.
source: Our approach allows large scale imaging of neurons across multiple hippocampal subfields, with known spatial and morphological relationships.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data throughout the study

claim: The microperiscope approach allows genetically controlled labeling of particular cell types.
source: In addition, our approach allows genetically controlled labeling of particular cell types, imaging of cellular structures such as dendrites and spines, and unequivocal tracking of functional and structural properties of the same cells across time, none of which are possible with existing electrophysiological approaches.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study

claim: The microperiscope approach allows imaging of cellular structures such as dendrites and spines.
source: In addition, our approach allows genetically controlled labeling of particular cell types, imaging of cellular structures such as dendrites and spines, and unequivocal tracking of functional and structural properties of the same cells across time, none of which are possible with existing electrophysiological approaches.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study

claim: The microperiscope approach allows unequivocal tracking of functional and structural properties of the same cells across time.
source: In addition, our approach allows genetically controlled labeling of particular cell types, imaging of cellular structures such as dendrites and spines, and unequivocal tracking of functional and structural properties of the same cells across time, none of which are possible with existing electrophysiological approaches.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the study

claim: Gradient index lenses have been developed for use in the hippocampus.
source: Several approaches making use of optical imaging have been developed for use in the hippocampus. These include gradient index lenses (Levene et al., 2004; Barretto et al., 2011), and cannulas that can be combined with both one-photon head-mounted microendoscopes (Ghosh et al., 2011; Ziv et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2016) and 2P imaging (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Dombeck et al., 2010; Sheintuch et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levene et al., 2004; Barretto et al., 2011

claim: Cannulas can be combined with both one-photon head-mounted microendoscopes and 2P imaging for hippocampal imaging.
source: Several approaches making use of optical imaging have been developed for use in the hippocampus. These include gradient index lenses (Levene et al., 2004; Barretto et al., 2011), and cannulas that can be combined with both one-photon head-mounted microendoscopes (Ghosh et al., 2011; Ziv et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2016) and 2P imaging (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Dombeck et al., 2010; Sheintuch et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2011; Ziv et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2016; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Dombeck et al., 2010; Sheintuch et al., 2017

claim: Existing optical imaging methods for hippocampus have been limited to horizontal imaging planes, making it difficult to image CA3 and DG.
source: These methods have been limited to horizontal imaging planes, making it difficult to image CA3 and DG, and intractable to image all three subfields in the same animal.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: It has been intractable to image all three hippocampal subfields (CA1, CA3, DG) in the same animal using existing optical imaging methods.
source: These methods have been limited to horizontal imaging planes, making it difficult to image CA3 and DG, and intractable to image all three subfields in the same animal.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: All optical imaging methods for hippocampus cause damage to the brain.
source: While all of these methods cause damage to the brain, and some require the aspiration of the overlying cortex, the damage is largely restricted to superficial hippocampus.
evidence: Based on knowledge of surgical procedures

claim: Some optical imaging methods for hippocampus require the aspiration of the overlying cortex.
source: While all of these methods cause damage to the brain, and some require the aspiration of the overlying cortex, the damage is largely restricted to superficial hippocampus.
evidence: Based on knowledge of surgical procedures

claim: Damage from existing optical imaging methods is largely restricted to superficial hippocampus.
source: While all of these methods cause damage to the brain, and some require the aspiration of the overlying cortex, the damage is largely restricted to superficial hippocampus.
evidence: Based on knowledge of surgical procedures

claim: The implantation of the microperiscope is inserted into the septal end of the hippocampus and necessarily causes some damage to the structure.
source: This contrasts with the implantation of our microperiscope, which is inserted into the septal end of the hippocampus and necessarily causes some damage to the structure.
evidence: Describes the surgical procedure

claim: Damage in the direction orthogonal to the transverse axis caused by the implantation of the microperiscope is similar to that caused by microprisms in cortex.
source: Damage in the direction orthogonal to the transverse axis caused by the implantation of the microperiscope is similar to that caused by microprisms in cortex (Andermann et al., 2013), as glial markers were found to decay to baseline levels with increased distance from the face of the microperiscope (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E and F, and supported by citation to Andermann et al., 2013

claim: Following successful implantation, the imaging fields were stable, and the same cells could be imaged up to 3 months later.
source: We showed that, following successful implantation, the imaging fields were stable, and the same cells could be imaged up to 3 months later (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Imaging planes should be at least 150 μm away from microperiscope face to avoid aberrant responses.
source: However, we emphasize that tissue damage caused by the microperiscope assembly to the hippocampus should be taken into consideration when planning experiments and interpreting results, and that imaging planes should be at least 150 μm away from microperiscope face to avoid aberrant responses.
evidence: Recommendation based on experimental observations

claim: The larger v2HPC microperiscope had slightly better optical properties than the smaller v1CA1 microperiscope, likely due to reduced beam clipping.
source: For example, the larger v2HPC microperiscope had slightly better optical properties than the smaller v1CA1 microperiscope (Figure 2), likely due to reduced beam clipping.
evidence: Demonstrated by optical measurements shown in Figure 2 and inferred from optical modeling

claim: Place cells are significantly less stable in the absence of reward, which may explain the lower lap-wise reliability in the current experiments compared to similar experiments using the same behavioral apparatus.
source: Recent work has found that PCs are significantly less stable in the absence of reward (Krishnan et al., 2020; Pettit et al., 2022), which may explain the lower lap-wise reliability in our experiments compared to similar experiments using the same behavioral apparatus (Go et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from comparison with prior studies and supported by citations to Krishnan et al., 2020; Pettit et al., 2022; Go et al., 2021

claim: Similar percentages of place fields were found as other optical imaging studies, despite using a strict criteria for PC inclusion.
source: However, we found similar percentages of place fields as other optical imaging studies, despite using a strict criteria for PC inclusion (see Materials and methods), and these properties did not change systematically as a function of distance from the face of the periscope (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: The functional properties of the hippocampal circuitry remained intact when using the microperiscope.
source: This provides further support that the functional properties of the hippocampal circuitry remained intact when using the microperiscope.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results

claim: PC characteristics measured might be altered in the presence of reward.
source: However, we note that it is possible that the PC characteristics we measured might be altered in the presence of reward, and that this decision should be taken into account when interpreting the results.
evidence: Speculative consideration of experimental design

claim: Several studies have tracked the spines of basal CA1 dendrites in vivo by imaging the dorsal surface of the hippocampus.
source: Several studies have tracked the spines of basal CA1 dendrites in vivo by imaging the dorsal surface of the hippocampus (Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Ulivi et al., 2019; Castello-Waldow et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Ulivi et al., 2019; Castello-Waldow et al., 2020

claim: Apical dendritic spines make up the majority of the input to CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Given that these spines make up the majority of the input to CA1 pyramidal neurons, there is a significant need for understanding their dynamics, and how the dynamics differ as a function of position along the somatodendritic axis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of hippocampal anatomy

claim: Isolated apical dendrites were tracked for up to 10 consecutive days using the microperiscope.
source: Using the microperiscope, we tracked isolated apical dendrites for up to 10 consecutive days (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Considerable addition and subtraction of spines was found across days, indicating dynamic turnover in apical dendrites.
source: We found considerable addition and subtraction across days, indicating dynamic turnover in apical dendrites (Figure 3H, I).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3H and I

claim: The majority of spines (76.5%) survived throughout the imaging period.
source: However, consistent with previous studies in basal spines (Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018), we found the majority of spines (76.5%) survived throughout the imaging period (Figure 3G).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and supported by citations to Attardo et al., 2015; Mizrahi et al., 2004; Pfeiffer et al., 2018

claim: The high survival fraction suggests that the daily turnover rates observed are reflective of a distinct pool of unstable transient spines, while the majority of spines are moderately stable.
source: This high survival fraction suggests that the daily turnover rates we observe are reflective of a distinct pool of unstable transient spines, while the majority of spines are moderately stable, and remain present over a longer timescale.
evidence: Inferred from the survival fraction and turnover data

claim: Some prior spine imaging results were obtained using super-resolution microscopy techniques that are more suited to capturing the dynamics of filipodia and small spines.
source: It should be noted that some prior results were obtained using super-resolution microscopy techniques that are more suited to capturing the dynamics of filipodia and small spines, and thus our results may reflect an inflated degree of stability (Attardo et al., 2015; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Ulivi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Attardo et al., 2015; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Ulivi et al., 2019

claim: The microperiscope is in principle compatible with super-resolution microscopy.
source: The microperiscope is in principle compatible with super-resolution microscopy, and future imaging studies that combine the two could characterize apical dendritic spine dynamics with improved accuracy (Attardo et al., 2015; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Ulivi et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative application based on the method

claim: Even in the absence of salient learning and reward signals, dendritic spines are dynamic and unstable structures.
source: Taken together, our results add to the increasingly appreciated idea that, even in the absence of salient learning and reward signals, dendritic spines are dynamic and unstable structures (Attardo et al., 2015; Chambers and Rumpel, 2017; Mongillo et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and supported by citations to Attardo et al., 2015; Chambers and Rumpel, 2017; Mongillo et al., 2017

claim: Understanding the nature and timescales of dendritic spine dynamics has significant implications for the reported instability of place cells.
source: Understanding the nature and timescales of these dynamics has significant implications for the reported instability of PCs (Mankin et al., 2012; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Ziv et al., 2013; Kentros et al., 2004; Kinsky et al., 2018; Mau et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to Mankin et al., 2012; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Ziv et al., 2013; Kentros et al., 2004; Kinsky et al., 2018; Mau et al., 2020

claim: Previous studies found gradients of connectivity in CA3.
source: Previous studies have found gradients of connectivity in CA3 (Claiborne et al., 1986; Ishizuka et al., 1990; Li et al., 1994; Ishizuka et al., 1995; Witter, 2007), suggesting that there may be functional gradients as well.
evidence: Supported by citations to Claiborne et al., 1986; Ishizuka et al., 1990; Li et al., 1994; Ishizuka et al., 1995; Witter, 2007

claim: Gradients of connectivity in CA3 suggest that there may be functional gradients as well.
source: Previous studies have found gradients of connectivity in CA3 (Claiborne et al., 1986; Ishizuka et al., 1990; Li et al., 1994; Ishizuka et al., 1995; Witter, 2007), suggesting that there may be functional gradients as well.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical findings

claim: The most proximal part of CA3 is functionally more similar to DG than to the rest of CA3.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have indeed found that spatial information and place field width vary as a function of distance along the DG-to-CA1 axis (Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Mankin et al., 2015), and that the most proximal part of CA3 is functionally more similar to DG than to the rest of CA3 (Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014

claim: The location of each neuron relative to the CA3 inflection point could be easily identified using the microperiscope.
source: The location of each neuron relative to the CA3 inflection point could be easily identified, allowing for unequivocal characterization of spatial information and place field width along the DG-to-CA1 axis across animals.
evidence: Describes the experimental approach

claim: The microperiscope allows for unequivocal characterization of spatial information and place field width along the DG-to-CA1 axis across animals.
source: The location of each neuron relative to the CA3 inflection point could be easily identified, allowing for unequivocal characterization of spatial information and place field width along the DG-to-CA1 axis across animals.
evidence: Describes the experimental capability

claim: Spatial information, but not place field width, differed significantly between CA1, CA3, and DG.
source: Indeed, we found that spatial information, but not place field width, differed significantly between CA1, CA3, and DG (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and I

claim: The high spatial resolution and ability to simultaneously record from cells across the DG-to-CA1 axis using the microperiscope approach strengthens the hypothesis of distributed spatial coding across, and within, hippocampal subfields.
source: Given the high spatial resolution and ability to simultaneously record from cells across the DG-to-CA1 axis using this approach, our results strengthen the hypothesis of distributed spatial coding across, and within, hippocampal subfields.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results

claim: Imaging of the transverse hippocampal circuit with microperiscopes will be a powerful tool for investigating hippocampal circuitry, structural dynamics, and function.
source: Combined with existing electrophysiological and imaging approaches, imaging of the transverse hippocampal circuit with microperiscopes will be a powerful tool for investigating hippocampal circuitry, structural dynamics, and function.
evidence: Inferred from the capabilities demonstrated in the study
